rebuttal.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments and would like to address the concerns regarding geographic diversity, dataset scale, and coverage of challenging real-world conditions in the following response. 

> (i) The dataset is geographically limited to three intersections within a single city Ingolstadt, Germany, which constrains its generalizability across diverse urban environments, traffic patterns, and regulatory frameworks. To enhance broader applicability, the authors should consider expanding data collection to major metropolitan areas such as Frankfurt, Munich, or Paris, which would provide more representative traffic scenarios and infrastructure variations. 

We acknowledge that our data collection is currently limited to three intersections within Ingolstadt, Germany. However, it is important to note that Ingolstadt is currently one of the few cities in Germany with a permanent, multi-intersection V2X infrastructure deployment at this scale, making it uniquely suited for collecting a dataset of this complexity. 

Similar deployments in other major cities such as Frankfurt, Munich, or Paris do not yet exist, primarily due to the considerable time, cost, and effort required for obtaining municipal permits, coordinating with stakeholders, organizing data protection concepts, retrofitting permanent infrastructure sensors and processing units across multiple intersections. These challenges are common across prior V2X datasets and represent a key bottleneck for real-world, large-scale data collection. To the best of our knowledge, no existing dataset provides multi-modal coverage of three distinct intersections (SOTA datasets have only one intersection) with multiple infrastructure nodes and multiple vehicles, even within a single-city context. 

Our selected locations were deliberately chosen along major arterial roads that reflect common traffic dynamics, infrastructure layouts, and occlusion patterns that are typically observed in many European metropolitan areas. These intersections exhibit high traffic density, diverse agent interactions, and complex geometry, making them representative of broader urban environments. 

The primary focus of our dataset is to provide diverse coverage of intersections with varying geometric layouts, rich sensor modalities, and a wide range of agent behaviors, all under realistic and high-traffic conditions. Additionally, it includes multi-modal data streams such as traffic light states, HD maps, and a digital twin environment—resources critical for robust and transferable V2X model development. 

Finally, despite covering only three intersections, our intersection-wise split (SIS) reveals a performance drop exceeding 30%, indicating real and meaningful generalization challenges even within a single city. This result underscores the meaningful diversity in sensor layouts, occlusion patterns, and traffic dynamics across the intersections, validating the benchmark’s ability to capture critical urban complexity. 

> (ii) With only 34 sequences totaling approximately 11 minutes of data, the dataset scale is quite small compared to established autonomous driving datasets (e.g., nuscenes, Waymo). This limitation may restrict the training of robust deep learning models and comprehensive evaluation.  

It is true that our dataset, at approximately 11 minutes of selected continuous recordings, is smaller in raw duration compared to large-scale autonomous driving datasets such as nuScenes or Waymo. However, these datasets are designed for single-agent perception in autonomous driving, where large-scale data collection is significantly more scalable and less complex. 

In contrast, our work focuses on cooperative perception, which introduces fundamentally different challenges and system requirements. In cooperative settings, multiple agents—vehicles and infrastructure—must coordinate, synchronize, and share sensor data to overcome occlusions and improve perception under realistic urban conditions. As such, direct comparisons with single-agent datasets are not straightforward and can be misleading. 

By contrast, each of our scenes involves 2 vehicles and 2–3 infrastructure units, together capturing data from 12 RGB cameras, 6 thermal cameras, and 6 LiDARs. This results in a diverse and distributed sensor coverage and enables the modeling of realistic multi-agent interactions. While the total length of selected scenarios is ~11 minutes, the effective multi-agent coverage exceeds 50 minutes, as each agent contributes a unique, temporally synchronized viewpoint. 

We believe that evaluating the value of a dataset solely by its duration is insufficient—scene complexity, sensor richness, agent diversity, and interaction density are equally critical. For example, our dataset features a high number of dynamic traffic participants, averaging ~105 objects per frame. In contrast, Waymo has ~60 objects per frame on average and does not capture cooperative multi-agent behavior. 

Relevant comparisons for our work are cooperative perception datasets such as V2XReal and TUMTraf-V2X. V2XReal provides ~13 minutes of data per agent at a single intersection; TUMTraf-V2X offers ~2 minutes of data with a single vehicle and a single infrastructure unit. Our dataset offers not only longer multi-agent coverage but also richer sensor modalities, multi-intersection settings, and greater geometry diversity, directly addressing key limitations in these prior efforts. 

We also acknowledge that expanding to larger environments and collecting more hours of cooperative multi-agent data would be beneficial. However, doing so at this level of complexity would require sustained cross-agency coordination, and long-term infrastructure access across cities, which are important factors that make such scaling inherently more difficult than for vehicle-only / single-agent datasets.

In summary, while we recognize the difference in total duration, we believe our benchmark fills a critical gap in the cooperative perception domain. It provides a realistic, high-fidelity setup that emphasizes agent coordination, occlusion handling, and generalization across rich, urban scenarios—characteristics not present in existing large-scale single-agent datasets. 

>  (iii) The paper lacks discussion of challenging conditions such as adverse weather, night-time scenarios, or emergency situations that are crucial for real-world deployment of cooperative perception systems. 

It is correct that our current dataset does not explicitly include adverse weather such as heavy rain, fog, or snow. Our primary goal in this release was to advance the field by addressing cooperative perception in complex, multi-intersection urban traffic environments. To that end, we prioritized capturing high-quality, synchronized sensor data across diverse urban scenarios involving multiple agents, infrastructure nodes, and traffic conditions. Coordinating and deploying such a system across multiple locations already required considerable logistical effort and operational resources. 

We see our work as a first but important step toward realistic cooperative perception benchmarks. While we demonstrate our framework across a range of challenging scenes, we fully agree that there is still room for additional dataset publications focusing specifically on adverse weather. Extending this system to other cities or integrating additional conditions such as adverse weather would require significantly more resources, planning, and long-term coordination—challenges we believe are best addressed in future research efforts. 

Our current dataset already covers a broad spectrum of lighting conditions, from full daylight through dusk to nighttime. Specifically, it includes 10 daytime scenarios, 5 under cloudy conditions, 6 moderate-light conditions, 5 late evening, and 8 nighttime scenes. We also provide 7 scenarios featuring mild to moderate glare, which can significantly challenge perception systems.

In terms of emergency and edge-case coverage, the dataset includes several safety-critical and rare real-world events, such as:

- A minor vehicle accident at an intersection (`20241126_0024_crossing1_08`)
- Police activity (`20241127_0025_crossing2_00`, `20241127_0024_crossing3_08`)
- Fire truck presence (`20241126_0008_crossing1_01`)
- Roadside assistance activity (`20241126_0024_crossing1_18`)
- An active construction zone (`20241127_0014_crossing2_00`, `20241127_0026_crossing2_08`)
- Moderate smoke from a vehicle in front (`20241127_0008_crossing1_00`)

These scenes provide valuable edge cases for evaluating the robustness of cooperative perception systems under irregular, unpredictable conditions. 

Finally, a unique strength of our benchmark is its built-in extensibility. We provide a geo-referenced high-fidelity CARLA map, which allows researchers to replay exact trajectories in the simulation. This enables systematic evaluation of cooperative perception under simulated adverse weather (e.g., rain, fog, snow) and varying visibility conditions in a controlled digital-twin environment. 

We see our dataset as a solid baseline for cooperative perception under typical weather conditions, enriched with critical real-world features such as multiple intersections, HD maps, a digital twin, traffic light states, and diverse sensor setups.

We are happy to address your questions regarding the inclusion of additional SOTA baselines in our evaluation, as well as the balance between dataset construction details and experimental analysis, in the following response.

> (1) It seems that the paper only includes three SOTA methods in Table 2. Since I am not very familiar with this area, is it possible to include more baselines? 

We agree that incorporating additional SOTA methods enhances evaluation and provides valuable insights. While our initial set of experiments included a wider range of models, for clarity and focus, we selected six representative approaches for the paper: three fusion baselines (NoFusion, EarlyFusion, LateFusion) to illustrate different fusion strategies, alongside three prominent SOTA methods (F-Cooper, V2X-ViT, and CoBEVT). summary.value: This paper introduces UrbanIng-V2X, a cooperative perception dataset collected across three urban intersections in Ingolstadt, Germany. The dataset features multi-vehicle and multi-infrastructure sensing with extensive sensor coverage including RGB cameras, thermal cameras, and LiDAR sensors from both vehicles and infrastructure. The work provides 34 sequences of 20 seconds each, with 712k annotated 3D bounding boxes across 13 object classes. The authors benchmark several state-of-the-art cooperative perception methods and propose novel dataset splitting strategies to evaluate generalization across different intersection layouts.

strengths_contributions.value:
+ The dataset provides an unprecedented combination of sensors including 12 RGB cameras, 17 thermal cameras, and 14 LiDAR sensors across vehicles and infrastructure, representing the most extensive real-world cooperative perception setup to date.
+ The introduction of Separate Intersection Split (SIS) strategy provides valuable insights into generalization challenges across different intersection layouts, revealing a significant performance drop ( > 30%) when models are tested on unseen intersections.
+ The meticulous sensor synchronization using UTC timing, precise calibration procedures, and motion compensation demonstrate strong technical rigor in data collection methodology.
+ The focus on urban intersections addresses a critical scenario for autonomous driving where cooperative perception can provide substantial safety benefits.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The dataset is geographically limited to three intersections **within a single city Ingolstadt, Germany**, which constrains its generalizability across diverse urban environments, traffic patterns, and regulatory frameworks. To enhance broader applicability, the authors should consider expanding data collection to major metropolitan areas such as Frankfurt, Munich, or Paris, which would provide more representative traffic scenarios and infrastructure variations.

summary.value: The paper proposes a first large-scale cooperative perception dataset that integrates multi-vehicle, multi-infrastructure, and multi-sensor modalities across multiple urban intersections. Compared to the previous dataset, the paper involves three unique interactions with two cars. Each car is equipped with a high-precision Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), a 128-ray high-end LiDAR sensor, and six Full High Definition (FHD) RGB cameras oriented in six directions, providing a full 360 FOV. At each intersection, 2 to 3 poles are installed, each equipped with 1 to 3 VGA thermal cameras. Additionally, six of the seven poles are equipped with a LiDAR setup, comprising a 64-ray midrange LiDAR and a 32-ray short-range blind-spot LiDAR. Detailed sensor descriptions and FOV coverage for infrastructure sensors are provided in the supplementary material. The dataset supports a broad range of cooperative perception downstream benchmark tasks, including 3D object detection, tracking, trajectory prediction, and localization. The paper benchmarks three different SOTA methods.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset seems to be a very useful resource compared to existing benchmarks. The paper includes digital twins and Traffic lights, which previous benchmarks do not have. The paper manages to fuse all the data together. The data collection is well documented. The paper is also clearly written. The proposed dataset can be applied to multiple tasks.
2. The paper provides a very detailed analysis of the proposed benchmark, with very clear visualization. 
3. The paper releases both code and dataset. The paper even provides a toolkit to run such dataset.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. It seems that the paper only includes three SOTA methods in the Table 2. Since I am not very familiar with this area, is it possible to include more baselines?
2. The analysis part of the experiment is relatively short. Is it possible to move some of the dataset construction details into appendix and include more experiment analysis to show the unique challenge of the proposed benchmark?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The paper provides code and a dataset.

final_justification.value: The authors provided additional information during the rebuttal sessions and have addressed my concerns. Given that I already provide a positive score, I decide to keep the rating.

title.value: UrbanIng-V2X: A Large-Scale Multi-Vehicle, Multi-Infrastructure Dataset Across Multiple Intersections for Cooperative Perception

abstract.value: Recent cooperative perception datasets have played a crucial role in advancing smart mobility applications by enabling information exchange between intelligent agents, helping to overcome challenges such as occlusions and improving overall scene understanding. While some existing real-world datasets incorporate both vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure interactions, they are typically limited to a single intersection or a single vehicle. A comprehensive perception dataset featuring multiple connected vehicles and infrastructure sensors across several intersections remains unavailable, limiting the benchmarking of algorithms in diverse traffic environments. Consequently, overfitting can occur, and models may demonstrate misleadingly high performance due to similar intersection layouts and traffic participant behavior. To address this gap, we introduce UrbanIng-V2X, the first large-scale, multi-modal dataset supporting cooperative perception involving vehicles and infrastructure sensors deployed across three urban intersections in Ingolstadt, Germany. UrbanIng-V2X consists of 34 temporally aligned and spatially calibrated sensor sequences, each lasting 20 seconds. All sequences contain recordings from one of three intersections, involving two vehicles and up to three infrastructure-mounted sensor poles operating in coordinated scenarios. In total, UrbanIng-V2X provides data from 12 vehicle-mounted RGB cameras, 2 vehicle LiDARs, 17 infrastructure thermal cameras, and 12 infrastructure LiDARs. All sequences are annotated at a frequency of 10 Hz with 3D bounding boxes spanning 13 object classes, resulting in approximately 712k annotated instances across the dataset. We provide comprehensive evaluations using state-of-the-art cooperative perception methods and publicly release the codebase, dataset, HD map, and a digital twin of the complete data collection environment via https://github.com/thi-ad/UrbanIng-V2X.
